query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of titanium to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will promote the formation of a stable, coherent network of nanoscale precipitates that enhance the alloy’s strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding a small atomic percentage of titanium during melt processing
generation.conditions: Samples produced via casting followed by standard thermomechanical processing; evaluated under cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, and corrosive environments relevant to aerospace fasteners
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent, titanium-rich nanoscale precipitates distributed along the lamellar boundaries
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion (thereby enhancing strength and reducing creep) and as barriers to corrosion pathways, while also improving local ductility through refined microstructural control
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased yield strength and ductility in tensile tests, improved resistance to room-temperature creep, and enhanced corrosion stability compared to the untreated alloy, while retaining the beneficial fine lamellar structure
generation.baseline: The performance characteristics of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy as reported in earlier work with its uniform, eutectic lamellar microstructure
generation.boundary: The benefits of Ti addition are expected within a narrow compositional window; excessive Ti may lead to precipitate coarsening or embrittlement, and the intervention is assumed to be effective under processing conditions similar to those used for the baseline alloy
generation.uncertainty: The optimal titanium concentration and the precise magnitude of performance improvements remain to be established; it is also uncertain whether the introduced precipitates will remain stable under prolonged extreme temperature cycling and corrosive conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one with a minor (optimized) addition of titanium. Subject both sets to identical thermomechanical processing. Evaluate microstructural evolution using electron microscopy, and test the samples under cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term creep loading, and corrosion environments that simulate aerospace conditions.
measurements: High-resolution TEM/SEM to detect and characterize titanium-induced nanoscale precipitates
Tensile testing to measure yield strength and ductility
Creep testing at room and elevated temperatures
Electrochemical and/or salt spray corrosion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the titanium-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (strength, ductility, creep resistance) and corrosion stability relative to the baseline, or if the expected nanoscale precipitates fail to form or become unstable under testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
